title: Motion with Integrals: Displacement and Distance
subject: AP Calculus AB

chunks.text: Integration runs the motion ladder upward: the integral of acceleration recovers velocity, and the integral of velocity recovers position.
Recovering a function by integration requires an initial condition to determine the constant of integration.
Velocity from acceleration is v(t) = ∫ a(t) dt + C, with the initial velocity fixing C.
Position from velocity is s(t) = ∫ v(t) dt + C, with the initial position fixing C.
Displacement is the net change in position over an interval, given by ∫ from a to b of v(t) dt = s(b) − s(a).
Displacement is a signed quantity: forward motion contributes positively and backward motion negatively, so they can partly cancel.
An object that returns to its starting point has zero displacement even though it traveled a real distance.
Total distance traveled is ∫ from a to b of |v(t)| dt, the integral of speed, and is always positive.
The absolute value in the distance formula makes backward motion add to the total rather than subtract.
To compute total distance, find where v(t) = 0, split the interval at those times, integrate v on each piece, and add the absolute values.
You cannot get total distance by integrating v over the whole interval, because backward motion would wrongly subtract.
Example: for v(t) = (t − 1)(t − 3) on [0, 4], the displacement is 4/3 m but the total distance is 4 m.
For a single position value, use s(b) = s(a) + ∫ from a to b of v(t) dt, avoiding the explicit constant C.
Example: with v(t) = 2t and s(0) = 5, the position is s(t) = t² + 5, so s(3) = 14.
Example: with a(t) = 6 and v(0) = −4, the velocity is v(t) = 6t − 4.
Constant acceleration a = −9.8 integrates to v = −9.8t + v₀ and then s = −4.9t² + v₀t + s₀, the kinematics equations.
The kinematics formulas from physics are antiderivatives of acceleration with initial conditions.
Displacement is the net signed area under the velocity curve, where below-axis regions count negative.
Total distance is the total area between the velocity curve and the time axis, counting every region positively.
Displacement versus distance is the motion form of net signed area versus total area under a curve.
Reading whether a problem asks for displacement, total distance, position at a time, or velocity from acceleration determines the correct setup.
Common errors include confusing displacement with distance, forgetting to split at direction changes, and dropping the initial condition.
